title: Five (May) Useful Tips for New Devs

posts.author: cradth
posts.body:
Hello everyone!
I'm Radian F (aka Cradth Helverd). I'm an indie dev who fell completely in love with the engine back in the RPG Maker VX Ace days. I've been a member of this forum for ten years now... and if you count the years I spent just reading through threads before officially signing up, I've been in the RM scene for about 13 or 14 years total.
Despite being here for over a decade, I've mostly been a professional lurker (guilty as charged! xD), quietly soaking in all the knowledge. Since I haven't been the most active poster, I wanted to change that and finally give something back to this amazing community.
No more long intros... let's dive right in. Since we just so happen to be in the month of May, welcome to
Five
May
Useful Tips for New Devs
.
1. Smart Asset Management
​
​
Spoiler:
Tips
Avoid "Enigmatic" File Names:
Resist the urge to leave your image files with names like "img1jshf_2025new05.png." Rename them as early as possible before you start using them in your project. It saves an immense amount of frustration later when you're eventing and trying to find a specific picture in a massive scrolling list.
Use Temporary Placeholders:
We often need numbered asset sheets or specific images to test plugins. If you get tired or creatively blocked while designing those graphics,
don't let it stall your game development.
Toss in a completely random placeholder image to keep the engine happy and keep pushing forward with your eventing. You can always overwrite the file with your final art later.
The Invisible Missing Image Fix:
We've all been there; the game randomly crashes because it's looking for a missing image file, and you have no idea why it's calling for it. Instead of letting frustration halt your project for weeks or months just because you don't know how to recode a plugin, there is an easy workaround. Just create a tiny, completely transparent 1x1 pixel PNG. Name it exactly what the error report is asking for, drop it in the folder, and keep devving without a hitch.
2. Movement & Loot Event Tricks
​
​
Spoiler:
Tips
Jumping Over Minor Obstacles:
To make exploration feel dynamic, you can set up Touch Events over small map details like stones, holes, or broken tiles. Use a Set Movement Route command to make the player automatically jump (X +/- 2 tiles or Y +/- 2 tiles). It makes exploration feel significantly smoother... After all, the Demon Lord shouldn't win just because your legendary hero got blocked or tripped up by a pebble. xD
Centralize Your Treasure Chests:
Instead of hardcoding the rewards inside every single treasure chest event on your maps, turn your loot tables into Common Events. By calling a common event-combining it with a variable and a conditional branch, of course-to handle the distribution, you can easily control the items/drop rates, prevent players from getting duplicate armors by accident, and balance your economy in seconds from one master list.
Fixing the "Teleport Sprite" Glitch:
In MV, when you change an event from having "None" as an image to a standard "3x4 grid" character sprite via an event page (like an NPC suddenly appearing), the engine will often default to the leftmost walking column, making them look frozen mid-step. To bypass this, give the event a blank, transparent "3x4 grid" character sprite as its default graphic, and select the middle column facing the direction you want. When you trigger the event to show the NPC, they will stand perfectly and naturally.
Note: I’m not entirely sure if this is a universal engine quirk or just a specific conflict on my end, so feel free to skip this trick if you've never run into this issue.
3. Unleashing Common Events
​
​
Spoiler:
Tips
The True Power of Common Events:
If you were like me during my first few years of RM making and didn't fully grasp what common events were actually for, here is the secret:
they are the ultimate time-savers for editing.
Imagine you have a simple command like "Show Picture 1: Actor1" used 50 times across different maps, and you suddenly decide to change it to "Show Picture 1: Actor2". If you evented those manually, you have to hunt down all 50 spots. If you put that line in a Common Event and just call it via Call Common Event, you can update all 50 locations in three seconds. Use them often!
Clear Names and Section Separators:
Once your project grows, you might end up with over a hundred common events. To save yourself from wasting time scrolling or worse- accidentally editing the wrong event, name them strictly by their purpose. A pro-tip for newcomers; you can use blank common events named "++++++++++" or "----------" as visual separators to neatly categorize your list into sections (e.g., UI, Mechanics, Cutscenes).
Mark Finished vs. Unfinished Work:
When managing a massive list of common events, use a quick visual tracking system right in the name slot. Try putting empty brackets "[ ]" or checkboxes "( )" before the name for WIP events, and a checkmark "[v]" once they are finalized. This tells you at a glance which systems are safe to leave alone and which ones you still need to revisit, polish, or finish later.
4. Playtesting Efficiently
​
​
Spoiler:
Tips
Enable Saving Everywhere:
If your game relies on "Save Crystals" or specific save points,
disable that restriction during playtesting
. Give yourself the ability to save anywhere from the menu. You don't want to lose progress or re-play long sections just because you need to jump back and check a quick fix.
Use Temporary Max Save Slots:
Even if your final game is only going to have 4 save slots, use a plugin or script during development to bump that up to 50. This lets you save at the start of every cutscene, boss battle, and major event. You can easily delete the plugin before your final release, but during development, it's a lifesaver.
Write It Down, Don't Trust Your Memory:
It sounds incredibly basic, but so many devs skip this. Keep a notepad handy during playtests. If you spot a tiny bug, write it down immediately. If you try to just "remember to fix it later," you
will
forget... and there is nothing worse than releasing your final build only for players to find an embarrassing bug in the opening map...
(Ask me how I know
.xD)
5. Strategic Backups
​
​
Spoiler:
Tips
Organize by Version:
Never hesitate to back up your project folder and rename it with clear, organized version numbers. Sometimes you'll install a new plugin or script that completely breaks things, or you'll realize an old plugin or script actually worked better. Having a clean history of older versions lets you easily retrieve old code or data.
Backup Daily:
Databases get accidentally deleted, files corrupt, and engines crash. Make it a habit to back up your work daily. If your current project file corrupts and you get stuck, you'll only lose a few hours of work instead of months.
Save Your Database History:
Backups aren't just for code- they save your writing, too. If you completely overhaul your weapons, enemies, or item descriptions and later decide the old versions were actually better, you can just open your old backup and copy the database files over instead of retyping dozens of lines from scratch.
*Shoutout to
@Solar_Flare
for pointing out that version control software can automate this entire backup process elegantly. Definitely give that a look if you want a more advanced setup!
That's all for now! I hope these general tips help out some of the newer devs and are worth the read. I'm just sharing what I've learned from my own trial and error over the years, so please have mercy if your own workflow looks a bit different!
That said...if you have your own tricks and advice based on your game dev journey, why not share them?
Drop a comment below if you want to add your own useful tips. At the end of the day, our goal is the same: let's banish the frustration of RPG Maker development and make it a fun, smooth experience for both newcomers and veterans alike.
Happy devving!

posts.author: Solar_Flare
posts.body:
There are a lot of good tips here, though I don't fully agree with most of them (but I do partially agree with most of them). The single best one is the "Write it down" tip. If you don't write it down, you
will
forget. I've forgotten to write it down many times and forgotten what I needed to fix.
The one thing I strongly
disagree
with is everything in point 5. You should really be using version control software for that, not manually making backups. It has all the advantages described under point 5 without needing to manually organize, label, and keep track of the versions. And if you, like me, make it a point to commit every time you have a complete and working change, then it's often like you're making
hourly
backups rather than daily ones (unless you were working on something big).

Thanks for the reply, I really appreciate it! You're completely right- version control software is definitely a better workflow. Doing it manually can definitely hog hard drive space. My goal with that point was just to offer a "raw and simple" manual method for absolute beginners who might feel overwhelmed by extra software.
That being said, I'm actually glad you brought it up! I've been using the traditional, manual way for my own project for years, so learning about these tools gives me some great insight to look into for myself, too.
Thanks again for the helpful suggestion!
